paragraphs.heading: Measuring the depths
paragraphs.text: Bathymetry is the study of how deep the floors of oceans, rivers and lakes lie, and of the shape of those floors. It is the underwater counterpart of topography. The first recorded evidence of people measuring water depth comes from Ancient Egypt, more than 3,000 years ago. The field also goes by names such as seafloor mapping and seabed imaging.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Bathymetric charts guide ships and mark hazards under the water. They usually show the shape of the bottom with contour lines called isobaths, along with selected depths called soundings. Depth data also helps in studying marine life near the bottom, in analysing coastlines, and in predicting currents and tides. Taking and analysing these measurements is a core part of modern hydrography and helps keep the world's shipping of goods safe. Yet in many places the seabed is still less mapped than the surface of Mars.

paragraphs.heading: From ropes to sound
paragraphs.text: Depth was first measured by depth sounding, which meant lowering a heavy rope or cable of known length over the side of a ship. This method gives the depth at only one point at a time, so it is less efficient. The ship's movement and the currents can also pull the line out of true, making it less accurate.

paragraphs.heading: Echoes from the seafloor
paragraphs.text: Today depth data typically comes either from systems that use light or from an echosounder, a sonar on a boat that sends a beam of sound down at the seafloor. The time the sound takes to travel down, bounce off the bottom and return tells the equipment how far away the seafloor is. Single-beam sounders were used from the early 1930s. Modern multibeam echosounders use hundreds of narrow beams, typically 256, in a fan usually 90 to 170 degrees wide, so a boat maps more seafloor with fewer passes. A computer corrects for the angle of each beam and for sound bending as it passes through water of uneven temperature, conductivity and pressure.

paragraphs.heading: Light and satellites
paragraphs.text: Some surveys use light instead, through LIDAR or LADAR systems that are usually airborne. Satellites help too. Satellite radar picks up subtle bumps and dips in the sea surface created by the gravity of underwater mountains, ridges and other masses. On average, the sea surface sits higher above undersea mountains and ridges than it does above trenches and abyssal plains.

paragraphs.heading: Depth compared to what
paragraphs.text: Depth figures are usually measured from a tidal reference level, called a datum. For deep water this is typically Mean Sea Level. Most data used for nautical charts is instead referenced to Mean Lower Low Water in American surveys and to the Lowest Astronomical Tide in other countries.
